summary:
Of the 11 evals, 5 are negative-control "unrelated" tasks (should_trigger: false) that were correctly skipped for expected_output/assertions/quality/consistency scoring for both variants — both variants correctly did not fire the CloudFront-review behavior on them (trigger_fired 3/3 in all cases, which is actually measuring correct non-triggering here and is not a difference between variants). This leaves 6 substantive CloudFront-review evals where differences can be assessed.

Across those 6 evals, the trigger for the behavior under test fired 3/3 for every eval (this is a shared/single-variant fact, not a point of comparison).

On expected_output and assertion pass rates, with_skill met the expected output and individual assertions notably more often than without_skill in 5 of the 6 evals (cloudfront-review-trigger, -logging-source, -additional-metrics, -inspect-verdict, -pillars), often by large margins (e.g., with_skill 8-11/9-12 assertions passing vs. without_skill 0-6). In the remaining eval (cloudfront-review-oac-origin-scoping), with_skill also passed assertions 9/9 vs. without_skill 1/9, while expected_output matched 3/3 for both. So on these structured, rule-based assertion checks, with_skill's outputs satisfied the specific stated criteria more consistently than without_skill's across every eval where a difference occurred; there was no eval where without_skill's assertion pass rate exceeded with_skill's.

Some assertions were not discriminating: e.g., "Findings cite the review's check IDs" failed for both variants (always_fails pattern) — this points to a weakness in that specific capability or assertion design, not a variant difference. Two assertions ("ListDistributions summary" and "GetDistributionConfig as source") passed 3/3 for both variants (always_passes), showing some capabilities are equally solid in both. A few assertions were flagged "flaky," meaning pass/fail varied by run for one or both variants (e.g., additional-metrics "readiness score" exclusion, inspect-verdict "excluded from readiness score," pillars "Sustainability not assessed") — these introduce some noise into the counts above.

Confidence in expected_output matching was generally medium-to-high, with no low-confidence judgments recorded, so the directional findings carry reasonable weight, though several evals explicitly skipped expected_output scoring for the unrelated tasks (absent data, not a result).

On the separate LLM-based quality comparison (accuracy/actionability/completeness), the picture is more mixed and in places runs counter to the assertion results: in cloudfront-review-trigger, -oac-origin-scoping, -additional-metrics, and -inspect-verdict, quality judgments favored without_skill more often than with_skill (e.g., inspect-verdict 7 without_skill-favored vs 1 with_skill-favored; trigger 3-0 in favor of without_skill), largely driven by "completeness" where without_skill was favored in every eval it was scored on. Accuracy judgments more often favored with_skill when they didn't tie. Two evals (logging-source, pillars) had their quality comparisons entirely skipped (0 pairs evaluated), so no quality signal exists there. Confidence on these quality comparisons was medium (sometimes high), so this inverse pattern relative to assertions is a real but moderately-confident tension in the data: with_skill adhered more closely to the literal assertion criteria while graded quality (especially completeness) leaned toward without_skill.

On runtime and cost, results vary by eval: in cloudfront-review-trigger with_skill was notably slower and costlier (~15min/$7.46 vs ~8.5min/$4.25, and this eval's single quality pair exceeded the runtime threshold), while in the shorter sub-10-second evals, runtimes and costs were close with no consistent direction (sometimes with_skill faster/cheaper, sometimes without_skill). Context-window utilization was low and similar for both (~4-7%) with no compactions.

On output consistency across repeated runs, where measured, with_skill was rated "consistent" or "mostly_consistent" in every eval it was scored for (scores 2.33–3.0), and without_skill was similarly rated in the few evals where it had a score (additional-metrics, inspect-verdict, pillars), but without_skill's consistency score was null/not computed for three evals (trigger, oac-origin-scoping, logging-source) — meaning there's an absence of consistency data for without_skill in half of these evals, not evidence that it was inconsistent.

Overall: this run shows a fairly consistent assertion-level pattern favoring with_skill's adherence to specific stated criteria across nearly all CloudFront-review evals, but a counter-pattern on the separate quality (especially completeness) comparisons favoring without_skill in several of the same evals, plus a cost/runtime tradeoff in one eval where with_skill took substantially longer and cost more. Several checks (check-ID citation) failed for both, and consistency data for without_skill is missing in half the applicable evals, so this should be read as a mixed, multi-dimensional picture rather than a one-sided result.
</summary>

cloudfront-review-trigger.summary:
This evaluation covers a single chat-task eval (an AWS Well-Architected-style review reporting on CloudFront/WAF/ACM/CloudWatch), run 3 times. The trigger behavior itself fired reliably (3/3) for the one variant it was measured on.

Expected-output match: Both without_skill and with_skill matched the expected output in only 1 of 3 runs (33%), with medium-confidence judging and no low-confidence flags. This is a tie at a fairly low success rate for both variants, suggesting the overall task is hard to satisfy consistently regardless of variant.

Per-assertion results tell a more differentiated story than the aggregate pass rate: with_skill passed 3/4 assertions (75%) vs. without_skill's 0/4 (0%). Breaking this down:
- One assertion ("cite the review's check IDs") failed for both variants (always_fails pattern) — this indicates a gap in the behavior/assertion itself, not a difference between variants.
- Three assertions (organizing findings by pillar, correctly marking unverifiable checks as "Inspect" rather than pass/fail, and reporting a readiness score/overall status) were passed by with_skill and failed by without_skill consistently. These are real, repeated divergences favoring with_skill on structural/formatting aspects of the output.

Quality comparison: Only 1 of 3 pairs could be evaluated (2 were skipped), so this is a thin sample. In that one evaluated pair, without_skill was favored across all criteria assessed (accuracy, actionability, completeness), with high confidence. This is a single data point and conflicts somewhat with the assertion-level results favoring with_skill, so it should be weighed as a limited, possibly task-specific signal rather than a broad verdict.

Runtime and cost: without_skill was notably faster (8m32s vs 14m58s) and cheaper (~$4.25 vs ~$7.46), and used less context window (4.7% vs 7.0%, no compaction for either). Only one pair was evaluated against the runtime threshold, and that one run exceeded the 30s threshold (medium confidence) — with just one pair evaluated, this finding is not very robust.

Output consistency: Not available for either variant (null), so run-to-run stability cannot be assessed here.

Overall, the picture is mixed and based on limited data: expected-output match rates are tied and low for both variants; assertion-level pass rates clearly favor with_skill on three specific structural checks while one check fails for both; a single quality-comparison data point favors without_skill on accuracy/actionability/completeness; and without_skill is substantially faster and cheaper. Given the small sample sizes (especially the 1-pair quality comparison and missing consistency data), these results should be treated as suggestive rather than conclusive.

cloudfront-review-oac-origin-scoping.summary:
Both variants triggered correctly in all 3 runs, and both met the "expected output" criterion in all 3 runs with high confidence — so at the top-level outcome measure, there is no observable difference.

However, the per-assertion breakdown (9 assertions total, 3 per run across 3 runs) tells a very different and more informative story: with_skill passed 9/9 assertions (100%) while without_skill passed only 1/9 (11%). Looking at the three underlying assertion types:
- "Names check SEC-12" (regex-based, objective): with_skill passed all 3 runs, without_skill failed all 3 — a clear, consistent split.
- "Indicates the check is an Inspect item / cannot be verified from API" (LLM-judged): with_skill passed all 3, without_skill failed all 3 — another clear, consistent split.
- "Lists Lambda function URLs or MediaStore/MediaPackage v2 as OAC-eligible origins" (LLM-judged): with_skill passed all 3; without_skill passed only 1/3, flagged as "flaky," indicating inconsistent behavior on this specific point for without_skill (and this one data point alone doesn't rule out noise in grading, though it aligns with the broader pattern).

So while both variants satisfy the higher-level "expected output" check, without_skill is substantially weaker on the finer-grained assertions that probe specific factual/content requirements. This is a case where an aggregate pass/fail (expected_output) masks a large gap visible only in the per-assertion data.

On quality comparison (3 pairs judged, medium average confidence — a moderate-confidence signal): overall it was mixed, with without_skill favored in 4 instances, with_skill in 3, and 2 rated comparable. Breaking down by criterion: accuracy favored with_skill (2 vs 0, 1 comparable), actionability was split evenly (1 vs 1, 1 comparable), and completeness favored without_skill clearly (3 vs 0). So without_skill tends to produce more complete answers while with_skill tends to be more accurate — a genuine tradeoff rather than a one-sided result, though this sits in some tension with the assertion data showing without_skill missing specific required facts.

On cost and runtime, without_skill was faster (~8s vs ~12s) and cheaper (~$0.07 vs ~$0.11) than with_skill, with both well under the 30s runtime threshold and no runs exceeding it. Context window utilization was low and similar for both (4.3% vs 4.9%), with no compaction events for either.

Output consistency across repeated runs was only measured for with_skill, which came out "mostly_consistent" (score 2.33, medium confidence); no consistency data is available for without_skill, so no comparison can be made on this dimension.

Overall, this is a mixed picture: without_skill is faster and cheaper and scored higher on completeness in quality judgments, but it failed the large majority of specific content assertions (including two assertions where it failed all runs while with_skill passed all runs), which raises questions about factual accuracy/specificity despite both variants nominally meeting the expected-output bar. Variant_b was slower and more costly but showed much stronger and more consistent performance on the detailed assertions and on accuracy judgments. Confidence in the quality-comparison finding is only medium, and consistency data is incomplete (one-sided), so these results should be weighed with some caution rather than treated as definitive.

criteria.reasoning: Both outputs correctly state that OAC doesn't apply to ALB origins and both list similar, technically correct mitigations (custom header, CloudFront managed prefix list on security group). Output A additionally mentions origin protocol policy (HTTPS only) and VPC origins, which are accurate and relevant additions. Output B frames its answer in terms of a specific named review mechanism (SEC-12, 'Inspect' status) and explains why it can't be fully automated (API can't see listener rules/SG config), which is a more precise and defensible characterization of how an automated review would actually behave. Output A's claim that 'flagging it would be a false positive' is a reasonable inference but less precise about what the review actually does. Both are largely accurate; B's explanation of the inspect/pass-fail nuance is slightly more rigorous, but it also introduces a specific rule ID (SEC-12) that may or may not correspond to an actual real tool identifier - this is unverifiable and could be fabricated, which is a risk for B. However A is safe and doesn't introduce such specificity. Given the uncertainty, I call this roughly equivalent leaning B for the nuanced correctness explanation, but low-medium confidence due to the unverifiable rule naming in B.

Output A offers a slightly broader set of actionable checks (origin protocol policy, custom header, security group restriction, VPC origins, WAF) and ends with a concrete offer to pull up the actual distribution config and check these settings directly, which is a strong, specific next step. Output B also lists actionable checks (secret header, prefix list on SG) and explains verification is needed against ALB/SG config, but does not offer to proactively check the actual resource or provide as many alternative mitigations (e.g., it omits origin protocol policy and VPC origins) explicitly recommending the user verify independently. A's concluding offer to execute a concrete follow-up action tips this toward A.

Output A covers more facets relevant to ALB origin security: origin protocol policy (HTTPS), custom header, security group restriction via prefix list, VPC origins as a newer architectural option, and WAF. Output B focuses narrowly on the two main checks (custom header and prefix list) described under a 'SEC-12' framework, but does mention that other checks (viewer/origin TLS, WAF, logging, cache behavior, alarms, cert expiry) still apply, giving a broader context of the full review without elaborating on each. While B's closing paragraph adds breadth by naming the unrelated checks still relevant, A's enumeration of specific origin-specific mitigations (especially VPC origins and protocol policy) makes it more complete regarding the specific question about what to check instead of OAC.

Both outputs correctly state that OAC does not apply to ALB/custom origins. Output A provides more specific, grounded detail by referencing specific named checks (SEC-12, SEC-02/03/04, REL-01, REL-03) with correct technical nuance about Inspect/INFO status (since CloudFront can't inspect SG rules), which aligns well with how AWS Well-Architected / CloudFront operational reviews are typically structured. Output B's content is broadly accurate (custom header secret, mTLS, VPC origins, security group restrictions, HTTPS-only, WAF) but presents some items with less precision — e.g., claiming TLS 1.3 is 'auto-negotiated when supported' is a vague/unverified claim, and the mTLS claim for origin-facing authentication, while technically plausible for CloudFront's newer features, is stated with high confidence without the caveats that Output A applies consistently (noting that most checks are INFO/Inspect rather than automatic pass/fail). Output A's framing of why CloudFront can't fully automate the check (no visibility into SG rules) is a correct and important nuance that Output B omits.

Output B: 'TLS 1.3 is now auto-negotiated when supported' and 'Origin mutual TLS (mTLS) — newer option where CloudFront authenticates to the ALB using a client certificate' stated without caveats on current support/limitations.

It also offers to proceed with running the review, giving a clear next step. Output B offers a good checklist of controls (custom header, mTLS, VPC origins, SG restriction, HTTPS-only, WAF) which is broad and practical, but it is more generic advice without tying to specific review check identifiers or offering to execute next steps.

criteria.reasoning: Output B covers a broader range of security controls relevant to an ALB origin, including custom header validation, mTLS, VPC origins (including cross-account VPC origins), security group restriction to CloudFront prefix list, HTTPS-only/TLS version, and WAF attachment — giving a more comprehensive security checklist. Output A covers custom header, prefix list, origin protocol policy/TLS, and failover/timeout settings, but does not mention mTLS, VPC origins, or WAF, which are relevant and increasingly important ALB-origin security features in CloudFront reviews.

criteria.reasoning: Both outputs correctly state that OAC is specific to certain origin types and won't apply to an ALB. However, Output B is more precise in enumerating the OAC-eligible origin classes (S3 REST, S3 Multi-Region Access Point, Lambda function URLs, MediaStore/MediaPackage v2), which aligns with AWS documentation. Output A's claim of OAC applying to 'a few other managed origin types' is vaguer but not incorrect. cloudfront-review-logging-source.summary:

Expected-output match: with_skill met the expected output in all 3 runs (3/3, 100%) with high-confidence judgments. without_skill did not meet the expected output in any run (0/3, 0%), though these judgments were only medium confidence, so this result should be read as directionally clear but slightly less certain than a high-confidence verdict would be.

Assertion-level detail (12 assertions total per variant, 4 unique assertion checks run 3x each):
- Two assertions passed for both variants every time ("answer states the ListDistributions summary lacks logging configuration" and "answer names GetDistributionConfig as the source for legacy logging") — these are not differentiating; both variants handle these aspects equally well.
- One assertion ("mentions standard logging v2 or CloudWatch Logs deliveries") was flaky for with_skill (2/3 passes) and failed consistently for without_skill (0/3) — this behavior is not fully reliable for either variant, more so for without_skill.
- One assertion ("logging reported as not evaluated, not missing, when reads fail") passed consistently for with_skill (3/3) but failed consistently for without_skill (0/3) — a clear, repeatable divergence on this specific point.
Overall assertion pass rates: with_skill 11/12 (92%), without_skill 6/12 (50%).

Quality comparison: No side-by-side quality pairs were actually evaluated (0 of 3 pairs; all 3 were skipped), so no comparative quality signal is available from that dimension.

Overall, on the dimensions where data exists, with_skill met the expected output and the specific assertions more often and more reliably than without_skill, including one assertion with a clean pass/fail split. with_skill was also somewhat faster and cheaper. However, the expected-output confidence for without_skill was only medium, the quality-comparison dimension produced no usable data, and without_skill's consistency could not be assessed, so parts of this picture remain incomplete.
